chapter.name: Lifelines of National Economy
chapter.blurb: Efficient transport, communication and trade are the lifelines of a modern economy. India's roadways, railways, pipelines, waterways and airways each serve distinct needs shaped by geography and cost; postal services and mass communication link people across the country; and growing international trade and tourism connect India to the world, with the balance of trade measuring the difference between what a country exports and imports.

scope_in.item: Transport as a prerequisite for trade and development; the three domains of transport -- land, water and air

Roadways: India's road network size (about 62.16 lakh km, 2020-21, second largest in the world); roads preceded railways; reasons roads have an edge over railways (lower construction cost, ability to traverse dissected/undulating topography and higher gradients such as the Himalayas, economical for short-distance/small-load transport with door-to-door service, and acting as a feeder to other transport modes)

Six classes of roads by capacity/authority: Golden Quadrilateral Super Highways (Delhi-Kolkata-Chennai-Mumbai, six-lane, includes the North-South corridor Srinagar-Kanniyakumari and East-West corridor Silchar-Porbandar, implemented by NHAI); National Highways; State Highways; District Roads; Other Roads (rural roads under the Pradhan Mantri Gramin Sadak Yojana); Border Roads (Border Roads Organisation, established 1960, strategic northern/north-eastern border areas)

Roads classified by construction material: metalled (cement/concrete/bitumen, all-weather) versus unmetalled (go out of use in the rainy season); the Atal Tunnel (9.02 km, built by the Border Roads Organisation, connects Manali to the Lahaul-Spiti valley year-round through the Pir Panjal range at about 3000 m altitude)

Railways: principal mode for freight and passengers, a great integrating force for over 150 years, the largest public sector undertaking in the country, first train Mumbai to Thane in 1853 (34 km), reorganised into 17 zones

Factors shaping railway distribution: favourable in the northern plains (level land, high population density, rich agricultural resources) despite river-bridging obstacles; unfavourable in the Himalayan mountains (high relief, sparse population, lack of economic opportunities); difficult in the hilly peninsular region (needs tunnels/gaps), western Rajasthan (sandy), Gujarat (swamps), and the forested tracts of Madhya Pradesh/Chhattisgarh/Odisha/Jharkhand; the Sahyadri crossed only through ghats/passes; the Konkan Railway along the west coast, and its problems (sinking track, landslides)
Railway problems: ticketless travel, theft and damage to railway property, unnecessary chain-pulling
Table 7.1, railway gauges: Broad Gauge (1.676 m, 63950 km route), Metre Gauge (1.000 m, 2402 km), Narrow Gauge (0.762 and 0.610 m, 1604 km), total 67956 km

Pipelines: a comparatively new transport mode, formerly used for water, now for crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas, and for solids converted to slurry; enables far-inland refineries (Barauni, Mathura, Panipat); high initial cost but minimal running cost; avoids trans-shipment losses/delays

The three important pipeline networks: (a) upper Assam oilfields to Kanpur (UP) via Guwahati/Barauni/Prayagraj, with branches Barauni-Haldia and Guwahati-Siliguri; (b) Salaya (Gujarat) to Jalandhar (Punjab) via Viramgam/Mathura/Delhi/Sonipat, with branches to Koyali and Chakshu; (c) the HVJ (Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur) gas pipeline, the first 1700 km cross-country gas pipeline, linking the Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields to fertilizer/power/industrial complexes in western and northern India, with the overall gas pipeline network since expanded to 18500 km

Waterways: cheapest, fuel-efficient, environment-friendly, suited to heavy/bulky goods; inland navigation waterways of 14500 km; the National Waterways Act, 2016 declared 111 inland waterways (including 5 earlier ones) as National Waterways

The five National Waterways: NW1 Ganga (Prayagraj-Haldia, 1620 km), NW2 Brahmaputra (Sadiya-Dhubri, 891 km), NW3 West Coast Canal in Kerala (Kottapurma-Kollam, Udyogamandal and Champakkara canals, 205 km), NW4 Godavari-Krishna stretches with the Kakinada-Puducherry canal (1078 km), NW5 Brahmani-Matai-Mahanadi delta channels and East Coast Canal (588 km); other used inland waterways: Mandavi, Zuari, Cumberjua, Sunderbans, Barak and the Kerala backwaters

Sea trade: 95 per cent of India's trade volume (68 per cent by value) is moved by sea; India's coastline is about 11098.81 km with 12 major and about 200 notified non-major ports; the major ports handle 95 per cent of India's foreign trade

Major sea ports and their distinguishing features: Deendayal Port/Kandla (tidal, first port developed after Independence to ease Mumbai's load after Karachi was lost to Pakistan, hinterland spanning J&K/Himachal Pradesh/Punjab/Haryana/Rajasthan/Gujarat); Mumbai (biggest port, natural well-sheltered harbour); Jawaharlal Nehru Port (decongests Mumbai, hub port); Mormugao (premier iron-ore-exporting port, about 50 per cent of India's iron ore exports); New Mangalore (exports iron ore concentrates from the Kudremukh mines); Cochin (natural harbour at a lagoon entrance); Chennai (one of the oldest artificial ports, ranked next to Mumbai in trade volume); Vishakhapatnam (deepest landlocked, well-protected, originally an iron ore export outlet); Paradwip (specialises in iron ore export); Kolkata/Shyama Prasad Mookerjee Port (inland riverine port, tidal, needs constant dredging of the Hooghly); Haldia (subsidiary port relieving pressure on Kolkata); V.O. Chidambaranar/Tuticorin (natural harbour, rich hinterland, trade with Sri Lanka/Maldives and coastal India)

Airways: fastest, most comfortable and most prestigious mode; can cover difficult terrain (high mountains, deserts, dense forests, long oceanic stretches); especially important for the north-eastern states (big rivers, dissected relief, dense forests, floods, international frontiers)
Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd: helicopter services to ONGC's off-shore operations and to inaccessible/difficult terrain (north-eastern states, interior Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand)

UDAN / Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS): 'Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik', a first-of-its-kind scheme globally by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, to jump-start the regional aviation market, promote regional connectivity, make flying affordable for the common citizen, and encourage airlines onto regional/remote routes through enabling policies and incentives

Communication -- postal network: the largest postal network in the world, handling parcels and personal written communication; first-class mail (cards and envelopes, airlifted, land and air) versus second-class mail (book packets, registered newspapers, periodicals, surface mail covering land and water); six mail channels for quick delivery in large towns/cities -- Rajdhani, Metro, Green, Business, Bulk Mail and Periodical Channel

Communication -- mass communication: radio, television, press and films as major means; Doordarshan as one of the largest terrestrial networks in the world; All India Radio (Akashwani) broadcasting in national/regional/local languages; newspapers published in about 100 languages and dialects, most in Hindi, then English, then Urdu; India as the largest producer of feature films in the world; the Central Board of Film Certification; the Digital India programme (IT/Indian Talent + IT/Information Technology = IT/India Tomorrow)

Telecom: India has one of the largest telecom networks in Asia; more than two-thirds of villages (excluding urban places) covered with STD facility; government extending 24-hour STD facility to every village at a uniform nationwide rate, enabled by integrating space technology with communication technology

International trade: the exchange of goods among people, states and countries is trade; a market is where such exchange happens; local trade (cities/towns/villages) versus state-level trade (between states) versus international trade (between countries, via sea/air/land); advancement of international trade as an index of a country's economic prosperity / its economic barometer; export and import as trade's components

Balance of trade: the difference between a country's export and import value; a favourable balance of trade is when export value exceeds import value; an unfavourable balance of trade is when import value exceeds export value; no country can survive without international trade since resources are space-bound

India's exports and imports: exports include gems and jewellery, chemicals and related products, agriculture and allied products; imports include petroleum crude and products, gems and jewellery, chemicals and related products, base metals, electronic items, machinery, and agriculture and allied products; India as a software-exporting giant earning foreign exchange through IT exports

Tourism as a trade: grown remarkably over the past two decades via government initiatives, infrastructure development and global branding; schemes to boost tourism -- Swadesh Darshan 2.0, Vibrant Village Programme, PRASHAD (Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual Heritage Augmentation Drive), Paryatan Mitra; tourism promotes national integration, supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits, and aids international understanding of India's culture and heritage
Types of tourism foreign tourists visit India for: heritage, eco, adventure, cultural, medical and business tourism; vast potential for tourism development across the country

concepts.name: Trade: local, state and international, and the balance of trade
concepts.description: How trade is classified by scope (local, state-level, international) and how a country's balance of trade is measured, illustrated by India's own exports and imports.
concepts.idea: Trade is the exchange of goods among people, states and countries; international trade specifically is trade between two or more countries, and is considered an index of a country's economic prosperity.
concepts.rule: The balance of trade is the difference between the value of a country's exports and imports: a favourable balance of trade means exports exceed imports, and an unfavourable balance of trade means imports exceed exports.
